posts.title: One angle hides three buyers: motivation, situation, objection
posts.hook: “Better sleep” is one angle. At least three different people are buying it.
posts.caption:
“Better sleep” is one angle. At least three different people are buying it.

Most teams write one ad per angle. That ad speaks to one kind of buyer, and when it slows down the whole angle gets blamed.

Split the angle three ways before you brief it:
Motivation: why they want it.
Situation: when they need it.
Objection: what stops them.

Each answer is a different person and deserves a different ad, starting with a different first shot.

Save this for your next brief. Follow @galvor.ai for one usable creative idea at a time.

posts.title: Data drop: what a batch of look-alike ads costs each ad
posts.hook: Six or more look-alike ads launched within three days: each got 48% less first-month spend.
posts.caption:
Six or more look-alike ads launched within three days: each got 48% less first-month spend.

That is from our analysis of new video ads launched May to Sep 2026 across brands we work with.

New ads that looked like many already running got 36% less. A proven message in a new look got 47% more.

Our reading: near-copies compete for the same people, and none gets a fair start.

Before your next batch, lay the first frames side by side. If two match, change one or hold it back.

Save this for launch day and follow @galvor.ai.

posts.title: Cyber Monday: separate what the discount did from what the creative did
posts.hook: A sale flatters every ad. Before you copy this weekend's winners, sort them.
posts.caption:
A sale flatters every ad. Before you copy this weekend's winners, sort them.

With a big discount on screen, weak ads sell too. Brief January from the sale leaderboard and you may be copying the discount.

Sort every sale ad into three piles: won before and during the sale, won only during it, lost even with the discount.

The first pile is your creative. The second is your offer. The third tells you what to leave out.

Save this and do the sort this week, while you still remember the details.

posts.title: AI in your creative team: who decides what
posts.hook: Before you add AI to a creative team, write down which decisions stay with people.
posts.caption:
Before you add AI to a creative team, write down which decisions stay with people.

Most teams are comfortable with AI doing the reading: tagging ads, counting what repeats, flagging what is slowing down.

The doubt starts when a tool changes spend or approves creative and cannot say why.

So agree the split first. AI reads and suggests, with reasons. A named person decides anything that spends or goes live.

That is how we built Galvor: it never touches the media budget.

Save the questions on the last slide for your next vendor call.

posts.title: Four early signs of creative fatigue, and the refresh-or-cut call
posts.hook: An ad shows it is tiring before the cost per order moves. Four early signs to watch.
posts.caption:
An ad shows it is tiring before the cost per order moves. Four early signs to watch.

Fewer people stay past the opening. The same people see it more often. Clicks drop while spend holds. Comments start saying “seen this”.

Then ask one question: is the message tired, or only the look?

If the message still works in other ads, refresh the look. In our analysis, a proven message in a new look got 47% more first-month spend.

Save the Monday check on the last slide. Follow @galvor.ai.

posts.title: Data drop: the slow starter. Why some ad styles look expensive early
posts.hook: The ad you cut in week two may have been fine.
posts.caption:
The ad you cut in week two may have been fine.

In our analysis of new video ads launched May to Sep 2026, some ad styles started about 35% dearer per order in their first two months and ended close to average over their life.

Early cost alone cannot separate a slow starter from a dud. You need a second signal: are people watching, and is the cost falling week on week?

Treat this as a pattern to test in your own account. Save the fair-trial checklist on the last slide and follow @galvor.ai.

posts.title: Five creative testing myths, and the fix for each
posts.hook: Five creative testing myths to leave in 2026, and what to do in place of each.
posts.caption:
Five creative testing myths to leave in 2026, and what to do in place of each.

A new script does not make a new ad. In our analysis, a new message over a familiar first shot got 16% less first-month spend.

More variations do not mean more learning. A test finds a winning part, and the ad around it will wear out. A clear no is worth paying for. And testing needs a fixed rhythm, or it waits for a free week that never comes.

Save the last slide: five myths, five fixes. Follow @galvor.ai.

Slide 4: myth three, the test found our winning ad. Slide 5: myth four, a losing test is wasted money. Slide 6: myth five, we test when we have time. Slide 7: five myths and five fixes in one list. Slide 8: follow @galvor.ai.

slides.headline: *5 creative testing myths* to leave in 2026
slides.sub: And what to do in place of each.

slides.kicker: Myth 1: “A new script makes a new ad”
slides.headline: less first-month spend for a *new message over a familiar first shot*
slides.sub: Fact: if the opening looks the same, change the opening.
slides.source: Source: Galvor analysis · new video ads launched May to Sep 2026

slides.headline: “Test *more variations* and you learn more”
slides.body:
Fact: if five things change between two ads, you cannot say which one mattered.

Change one thing per test. You get fewer ads and clearer answers.

slides.headline: “The test found our *winning ad*”
slides.body:
Fact: an ad wears out. What lasts is the part that made it work, such as the opening or the person on screen.

Name the part, then reuse it.

slides.headline: “A losing test is *wasted money*”
slides.body:
Fact: a clear no stops you briefing the same idea again and again.

It is only wasted if nobody writes it down.

slides.headline: “We test *when we have time*”
slides.body:
Fact: testing that waits for a free week does not happen.

Give it a fixed rhythm. Ours is a loop that runs every two weeks.

slides.headline: Five myths, *five fixes*
items: New script: change the first shot too
More variations: change one thing
Winning ad: name the winning part
Losing test: write down the no
When we have time: fix a rhythm

slides.headline: *5 questions* to ask any AI marketing tool about your data
slides.sub: Ask them before you connect the ad account.

slides.headline: What exactly do you *read*, and can you change anything?
slides.body:
Ask for the list of permissions in writing.

Reading performance data is one thing. Editing budgets or ads is another, and you should know which you are granting.

slides.headline: Is our data used to *train* anything others benefit from?
slides.body:
What your ads have taught you was paid for by your brand.

Ask whether it feeds models, benchmarks or suggestions that other brands, including rivals, will see.

slides.headline: *Where* is it stored, and who can see it?
slides.body:
Ask which country the data sits in, and which people at the vendor can open your account.

A vendor who knows will answer in a line.

slides.headline: Which *other providers* does it pass through?
slides.body:
Many tools send data on to outside AI models.

Ask for the list, and whether those providers keep your data or learn from it.

slides.headline: What happens to it when we *leave*?
slides.body:
Ask how you export what the tool has learned about your brand, and how deletion is confirmed.

Get the time frame into the contract.

slides.headline: Send these *five* before the demo
items: What can you read, and what can you change?
Does our data train anything others use?
Where is it stored, and who can see it?
Which other providers receive it?
How do we export and delete when we leave?

slides.headline: Ask every vendor. *Ask us too.*
slides.sub: Save the five questions for your next demo.
